opus-5.5.text:
I think that claim is partly true, but I'd frame it a bit differently.

If you compare robotics with areas where reinforcement learning has recently worked really well, like math or coding, the contrast is real. In math, you get an answer and you can check whether it's right. In coding, you run the unit tests and they pass or they fail. That signal is clean, cheap, and you can get millions of them. That's a big reason reasoning models improved so quickly.

In the physical world it's messier. Say you ask a robot to fold a shirt. What counts as success? Is a slightly wrinkled fold okay? What if it folded the shirt but knocked a cup off the table along the way? A lot of what we care about is fuzzy, and it depends on human preference and context. And even when success is clear, like "did the object end up in the bin," checking it usually needs a person watching, or some instrumentation of the environment, and that doesn't scale the way a compiler does.

But I don't think embodied intelligence fundamentally lacks feedback. In some sense physics is the most honest verifier there is. If you grasp something badly, it falls. If your walking controller is wrong, the robot falls over. Feedback is everywhere. The problem is that it's expensive to collect, slow, sometimes unsafe, and hard to turn into a scalar reward without a lot of hand engineering.

So I see a few ways forward.

The first is simulation. In locomotion, for example, we can define rewards fairly well and train at massive scale in simulation, and that's why legged robots have gotten so good over the past few years. The sim-to-real gap is still a challenge, but for many problems it's manageable.

The second, which I'm quite excited about, is using foundation models as the verifier. A vision-language model has a lot of common sense about what a successful outcome looks like. It can look at the scene and say "the shirt is folded" or "the task is not complete." It's not perfect, but it's improving fast, and it turns a fuzzy human judgment into something we can query automatically. That starts to close the loop.

The third is that we may not need a perfect verifier for everything. Humans don't get clean rewards either. We learn from imitation, from watching others, from noisy self-assessment. A mix of pretraining on large amounts of data, imitation, and then reinforcement learning with imperfect but scalable feedback may be enough.

So my view is: yes, the lack of cheap, verifiable rewards is one of the key bottlenecks, and it's a big reason robotics hasn't had its "o1 moment" yet. But I see it as an engineering and scaling problem we're actively solving, not a fundamental wall.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation can contribute alongside pretraining and imperfect feedback, but does not state that imitation-learning data alone already provide sufficient learning signals.

r002.rationale: It describes physical-world feedback as hard to turn into a scalar reward and says this requires substantial hand engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the claim has a kernel of truth, but it's often stated too strongly, and it misses where the real difficulty lies.

Compare it with the domains where reinforcement learning and large-scale training have worked spectacularly. In Go, the game tells you whether you won or lost. In code generation, you run the unit tests and they pass or they fail. In math, you check the proof. Those signals are cheap, exact, and you can get millions of them. That's the world people have in mind when they say embodied intelligence lacks verifiable feedback.

But in robotics, the physical world is actually the ultimate verifier. If I ask a robot to pick up a cup and put it on the shelf, either the cup is on the shelf or it isn't. Gravity doesn't lie. Did the robot fall over? Did the door open? Those outcomes are completely objective. So the signal exists. The problem is not that it's unverifiable, it's that it's expensive and slow to collect, and it's often sparse. You might need a long sequence of actions before you find out whether you succeeded, and running that trial in the real world takes seconds or minutes, and may break your hardware, instead of taking microseconds on a GPU.

That's why simulation has been so central in my work. Simulation gives you a verifiable signal at scale. We trained legged locomotion controllers almost entirely in simulation, where the reward is clear: did the robot move forward, did it stay upright, how much energy did it use. Then we transferred to the real robot. The verification was there; the engineering challenge was closing the sim-to-real gap so that what's verified in simulation stays true in the physical world.

Where the claim does hold is for the fuzzier tasks. If the instruction is "tidy up the kitchen," what counts as tidy? If it's "fold the laundry nicely," how nice is nice enough? There the reward is a judgment, not a measurement, and that's where we start to lean on learned reward models, vision-language models acting as judges, or human preferences. These are noisier, but this is exactly the same situation language models face with open-ended text, and that community has made progress with it. I don't see why robotics can't borrow the same tools.

So my view is that embodied intelligence has very good feedback for the low-level, physical outcomes, and increasingly workable feedback for the high-level, semantic ones. The bottleneck is the cost of collecting experience in the real world, not the absence of a signal. And if you look at the trend, the combination of better simulators, world models that let you imagine outcomes, and foundation models that can evaluate behavior from video, is steadily driving that cost down. I'm quite optimistic that the "no feedback" argument will look much weaker in a few years than it does today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses objective physical outcomes and costly real-world feedback, but does not mention imitation-learning data or say that it already provides sufficient learning signals.

r002.rationale: It identifies fuzzy tasks such as tidying or folding laundry as difficult to evaluate because the reward depends on subjective judgments rather than clear measurements.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim is too broad. In embodied intelligence, many tasks have very clear, verifiable feedback. If a robot is trying to walk, did it move forward without falling? If it is picking up an object, did the object actually leave the table? Those are outcomes we can measure.

The harder question is whether that feedback is sufficient for learning. A robot might fail to complete a task, but that failure alone doesn’t tell it which action was wrong or how to improve. And collecting another attempt in the physical world takes time and can cause wear or damage.

So I would distinguish between having a verifiable outcome and having a useful learning signal. For narrowly defined tasks, we often have both. For long, open-ended tasks—say, tidying a home—the criteria are more complicated, and success may depend on human preferences. The challenge is making feedback informative, scalable, and cheap enough to support learning, rather than assuming embodied intelligence has no clear feedback at all.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes measurable outcomes from useful learning signals and says task failure may not show how to improve. It does not state that imitation-learning data already provide sufficient learning signals.

r002.rationale: The response notes that open-ended task criteria can be complicated and depend on human preferences, but it does not identify expressing an embodied task as a reward function in reinforcement learning as a difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between feedback that is difficult to obtain and feedback that is fundamentally unclear. In robotics, many tasks have very concrete success criteria. Did the robot pick up the object? Did it reach the destination without falling? Those outcomes are observable and verifiable.

The challenge is that this feedback can be sparse and expensive. If a robot fails to pick something up, that tells you the task failed, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you which part of its behavior caused the failure. And collecting another thousand attempts in the physical world takes time and can damage hardware.

For open-ended tasks, the criteria become more complicated. If you ask a robot to tidy a room, you have to specify what counts as tidy, which objects it can move, and what it must avoid. Human preferences matter there.

So I wouldn’t say embodied intelligence lacks clear feedback. I’d say we need better ways to turn measurable outcomes, physical observations, and human judgments into useful learning signals. The difficulty is making that process efficient and scalable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses observable outcomes and learning signals, but does not say that imitation-learning data already provide sufficient signals.

r002.rationale: It notes that defining criteria for open-ended tasks is complicated, but does not identify expressing embodied tasks as reward functions in reinforcement learning as a difficulty.
